speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of personal privilege, my attention has been drawn to an article that appeared in

Question of Privilege
the Ottawa Citizen of Thursday, October 4. The article is entitled "Liberal M.P. Angry Over P.M.'s Reply". It reads in part as follows:
Reid Scott (NDP-Toronto-Danforth) complained in the commons today about a reply by Prime Minister Diefenbaker to a civil service appeal against the current government wage freeze.
Mr. Scott asked what consideration the government is giving to a request by the civil service association of Canada, now meeting in Vancouver, for immediate rescinding of the freeze on salary increases for 50,000 clerical and semi-professional workers. Mr. Diefenbaker said that when the government is in a position to make an announcement, it would do so.
My question of personal privilege is this. I do not really mind the people of Canada being informed that the Prime Minister will not deal with this subject, but when it is at the expense of my being publicly called a Liberal M.P. it is almost too great a price to pay.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CLOSING OF POOL
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture arising out of his interest in getting money into the hands of the farmers. In view of the much lower price being received by producers of Durum wheat, and in view of the low stocks of Durum on July 31, can the minister say whether the 1961-62 Durum account can be closed out at an early date

and final payment, which farmers expect should be close to 75 cents per bushel, made immediately?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CLOSING OF POOL
speechtext: The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of this question. I appreciate his statement concerning the minister's interest in raising the income of farmers. I should like to inform him that the 1961-62 Durum pool will be closed as soon as possible. I draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that of the approximately 10.5 million bushels of Durum wheat delivered during the 1961-62 crop year, 21.9 per cent of 2.3 million bushels were delivered by producers during the last month of the crop year. These late deliveries occurred notwithstanding the Canadian wheat board's efforts to encourage producers to deliver their Durum earlier to permit the board to take advantage of the active demand for this type of wheat. Every effort is being made by the board to market supplies of Durum wheat remaining in the 1961-62 pool in order that the pool can be closed as quickly as possible.

Mind you, the political complexion is not entirely what I would have wished, but after all they do represent a cross-section of the Canadian people. I am sure they will prove to be responsible and conscientious as has been in the case in each of the other parliaments in which I have had the privilege of serving.
Today I intend to deal with three subjects; first of all the emergency program, then the commonwealth conference and finally Canada's position in the world. Before doing so, however, I think it would be fair comment on my part to say that on each of these subjects, regrettably, the Leader of the Opposition has seen fit to take an attitude which can only be described as abusive.
With regard to the emergency program, in his speech the other night the Leader of the Opposition accused the Prime Minister of this nation of fraud and misrepresentation. In the first place those charges were not true, and in the second place it was not fitting that any leader of any party in this house should make a virulent attack of that kind. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
I suggest that any reasonable Canadian will admit that the government took the proper course in all the circumstances.
Then a few words about the commonwealth conference. It was called, of course, to consider the implications of the United Kingdom joining the European community. It should be remembered at all times that negotiations between Great Britain and the community


were not completed and are not completed yet. That was the situation in which the conference met.
It was impressive and inspiring, Mr. Speaker, to sit at that table around which were gathered the representatives of the 15 free and equal members of the commonwealth as well as the prime minister of Rhodesia and Nyasaland and the prime minister of Uganda, who did not speak but was sitting there at the table. His country will be free before the end of the present month, and has asked to join the commonwealth. That request was granted at the conference.
The prime minister of British Guiana was sitting in the room as well and the representative of Kenya, the prime minister of Singapore, the prime minister of Malta and the representative of Mauritius. These men were there although they did not participate in the proceedings, but in a very short time their countries will be free and full fledged members of the commonwealth. This is something that would have inspired anyone in this chamber today if he had had the privilege of attending such a conference.
In Canada it is almost forgotten that there are two features of the implications of Great Britain joining the European community. First and foremost are the political implications and, second, there are the trade implications. I believe that the political implications are more important, and to my surprise that was the position taken by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom at the conference.
The political implications, what follows if the United Kingdom goes into Europe after 300 years of refusing to take that step, are of prime importance. Of course a good deal will depend on the extent to which Europe becomes a united states of Europe, with a common parliament and a common foreign policy, or perhaps becomes simply a loose alliance. There will be a difference in effects depending upon the type of European community that develops. But in the conference there was a general concern on the part of every prime minister because of the possible effect on the commonwealth. That is very clearly set out in paragraph 15 of the communique, which was in these words:
At the same time the representatives of various commonwealth governments expressed anxieties about the possible effects of Britain's entry into the European economic community. They trusted that, should there be closer association between Britain and Europe, it would not be allowed, as it developed, to weaken the cohesion of the commonwealth or its influence for peace and progress in the world.
Great value was placed on the commonwealth by every prime minister there, from the one representing the oldest former colony,

our own Prime Minister, to the representative of the newest, Trinidad and Tobago. Such value was properly placed on the commonwealth because today it is the finest association of nations in the world. It embraces representatives of all races and creeds, and I do not believe there has ever been anything quite like it in the history of the world.
There are great traditions behind it. Twenty one or twenty two years ago the commonwealth stood alone in saving civilization. While we were in London we attended a memorial service for the young airmen who lost their lives in the battle of Britain, including Canadian airmen. These associations really go much too deep in Canada for words, and they mean so much also to all the other members of the commonwealth.
If the commonwealth should be weakened or brought to an end, think of what would result as far as Canada is concerned. Think of the increased difficulty we would have in preventing our country from being drawn completely into the American orbit. Canadians from coast to coast must keep this fact in mind, just as our ancestors have had to. The Asiatic countries of the commonwealth do not want to be simply cast aside, and they fear that might be the result. With regard to the African countries of the commonwealth, in the negotiations at Brussels Britain obtained the right for them to become associate members of the European community, which would be of great benefit to them economically. But these African countries, Nigeria, the greatest country in Africa with the largest population, Tanganyika, and Ghana, refused to accept associate status because they were afraid it would make them economic colonies of Europe and would interfere with their development as sovereign nations. At the conference they turned down that offer.
Our Prime Minister has always been a commonwealth man. At the conference he made a most statesmanlike address which received from all the other prime ministers far greater applause than that accorded to the remarks of any other prime minister. The opposition talks about Canada's standing being ruined. One had only to sit at that conference table to see the standing that Canada has among the commonwealth nations. That is partially as a result of the stand our Prime Minister took a year ago on the question of South Africa, but today Canada stands in the very front rank so far as admiration and friendship are concerned on the part of the other members of the commonwealth.
The Leader of the Opposition showed no concern in his speech about what happens to the commonwealth. He whined about strengthening Europe, and said that Britain should
The Address-Mr. Green get into Europe to strengthen it. Europe is not such a weak little sister today. The NATO organization is probably the strongest military alliance there has ever been in peacetime. Europe does not need strengthening in that sense. She is just as strong as she would be if the British were to go into the common market.
Then he charged that our Prime Minister had told the British "You have to decide on whether you keep the commonwealth or whether you go into Europe". There was no such position taken by the Canadian Prime Minister. He made it clear from the start the decision was a decision for the British themselves. You know, the hon. member for Davenport seems to think he has all the answers. He always comes running along with a slick solution for everything. Speaking in January, here is what he said about Canada's attitude toward Britain and the European community:
.. . the government should have been urging and supporting Britain's application.
In other words we should have been shoving the British into the European community in the same way he wanted to shove a lot of maritimers up into Ontario.
Then there are the trade implications, and they are very far reaching for every member of the commonwealth. The Prime Minister of Canada spoke for Canada, which was his duty. I have not the time to quote from paragraph 16 in the communique, but it contains reference to the items in which Canada was interested. The other night the Leader of the Opposition said our Prime Minister should have been approving what the British government put into the communique. Paragraph 12 was the British case. We were criticized because our Prime Minister did not come down in complete support of the British representations. He was there to represent Canada.
Our main concern in the trade field today is foodstuffs. There is to be a procedure set up in the community under which there will be a tariff against many of Canada's foodstuffs, imposed by way of a levy. This levy will be put on by the community's civil servants, not by the British government. The money they get will be paid out by those same civil servants. As the prime minister of Australia pointed out, this is a strange sort of arrangement. This is the type of operation planned in regard to these tariffs to maintain artificial prices on foodstuffs produced in the countries of the European community. Make no mistake about it; as yet the community is inward looking. Let Canadians not expect the approach of the community, certainly on agricultural questions, to be in the direction of cutting down on the restrictions.

The Address-Mr. Green
Canada is vitally interested in raw materials. Negotiations on these items have not yet been completed. We are hoping for a nil tariff on many of our materials such as aluminum, lead and zinc. In so far as processed goods are concerned, the negotiations have not even started in connection with many of them. For example canned salmon, one of the items which come under this heading, has not been considered. In so far as manufactured goods are concerned, there have been tentative arrangements but we are hoping there will be some more favourable conditions worked out.
There has been a great deal of work done here in Ottawa, in Brussels, in London and in the committees of the commonwealth conference by Canadians. We have pointed out ways in which the position could be improved from the point of view of Canada. For one thing, we believe a great deal of help could follow from the United States trade plan. We would like to see negotiations under the United States trade plan take place with the community and with other nations as much as possible simultaneously with negotiations between Great Britain and the European community. We believe if that could be done the result would be very much more beneficial all around, and it would be much more possible to get lower tariffs.
The Prime Minister's trade proposal had that same objective in mind. He suggested that commonwealth countries should call for a trade conference and invite all the members of the commonwealth, the members of the community, the members of the European free trade area, the United States, Japan, and other like minded countries. This proposal received quite extensive support, for example from the president of Pakistan, the prime minister of Tanganyika, the prime minister of India, and qualified support from others. It was applicable whether or not Great Britain went into the community. I believe that eventually this plan of having a wider conference will be the one which will be followed. I also believe it will be in the best interests of Canada.
The United Kingdom now goes back to resume negotiations in Brussels, and arrangements have been made for a continuation of the consultations with commonwealth, countries. In so far as Canada is concerned, Canada will co-operate regardless of what happens. Canada will also do her best to maintain and strengthen the commonwealth. I have here a very significant paragraph from the speech from the throne which reads:
... the government will spare no effort to safeguard the interests of Canada while preserving the unity and strength of the commonwealth as a whole.

Then, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word or two about Canada's position in world affairs. During the discussions in London we had quite a wide ranging talk on world affairs. There the Prime Minister and I suggested that the commonwealth should back up the United Nations in its efforts to settle the Congo problem, and that there should be a statement issued by the conference on the question of disarmament. Both of these suggestions were accepted. If hon. members will refer to the communique they will find that both these subjects have been dealt with. It is a great help in trying to get some disarmament plan worked out to have the unanimous endorsation of these 15 members of the commonwealth.
I really do not believe it is necessary for me to answer those charges that Canada's position in world affairs have been ruined by the present government. I know they were just cheap political talk. Now that the election is over I hope these attacks will cease and that once again the opposition will get in and try to help maintain Canada's position in the world.
I mentioned our position in the commonwealth and in the field of disarmament. Today Canada stands as one of the leaders, perhaps the leading nation of the world, in efforts to bring about disarmament, to bring about a cessation of nuclear tests and to deal with the question of radiation and the horrible effects on humanity which this radiation may bring about.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
-and to the campaign
launched by the Social Credit leaders who momentarily succeeded in deceiving the good faith of a number of voters. The reasons for Quebec's dissatisfaction with the Conservatives are well known.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And with the Liberals too.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The paradox in our political situation resides in the fact that a great number of Quebecers, by voting for Social Credit, as a protest against the Conservatives, only succeeded in keeping them temporarily in power. That, and also to a great extent the campaign of make-believe and deceit of the Social Credit leaders in the province of Quebec explains the paradox.
The first illusion which the Social Credit leaders tried to create in Quebec was that Alberta and British Columbia had each become a paradise on earth and that Social Credit was still very popular there and that moreover their party would succeed in having a great number of members elected outside the province of Quebec.
Such frequent allegations had their effect on June 18 last, but they were refuted that very same day, because, as we all know by now, Social Credit came in fourth place in British Columbia, far behind the other parties, with only 14 per cent of the votes, in comparison to 24 per cent in 1957 and 27 per cent in 1953.
In Alberta, Social Credit obtained only 29 per cent of the votes in 1962, whereas it had 38 per cent in 1957 and 41 per cent in 1953, when it came first among the parties.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How much for the Liberals?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
On the morrow of the election, those who had believed in the trickery of Social Credit had to realize that they were alone and isolated in the province of Quebec, like our friends on the left, and that they had simply contributed to the election and maintenance in power of the Conservative party. Thus they had lost everything, even their votes.
Mr. Speaker, turning now to other matters, I should like to discuss the Social Credit doctrine as explained during the election cam-
The Address-Mr. Chevrier paign, as set forth in the book entitled "Real Caouette vous parle" and as put forward in this house by the member for Villeneuve.
According to the latter and his colleagues, all our economic problems arise from an only cause: under the present system, there is a chronic and permanent lack of purchasing power; in other words, incomes are lower than the amount of goods produced, with the result that those goods cannot be entirely consumed. This is what he says at page 83 of his book:
-total salaries amount to $25 billion. Now, with a national revenue of $25 billion, how can people buy for $38 billion. Such is the current problem today.
In my opinion, this is a gross mistake on the part of Socred leaders, because we actually buy every year our total national production. If the member for Villeneuve would only examine a little more closely the statistics pertaining to our national accounting, he would soon realize his elementary mistake. In fact, he compares the disposable personal income with the total income or with the national production. In 1961, for instance, this disposable income on the part of the general public amounted, as he said, to about $25 billion, but personal income accounts for only a part of the total income of the nation. The government and the commercial concerns also have incomes which they spend, in turn, for services or investments. In this perspective, the disposable personal income can only be compared with the consumers' expenses, which amounted to slightly more than $24 billion in 1961.
On the other hand, had the hon. member for Villeneuve examined more carefully the national accounts, he would have realized that if personal income came to some $25 billion in 1961, the total income, or the national product, was close to $37 billion, and the total national expenses also amounted to almost $37 billion. Therefore, it is clear that we buy each year all that we produce, and that the mistake made by the Social Credit leaders simply consists in comparing a part with the whole and in being surprised at finding that this part is less than the whole.
Besides, if the explanation given by the Socred leaders was of any value, it would follow every country would be continuously facing mass unemployment and economic crises, since disposable personal income is always lower than the national product by a several billion dollars margin. How is it then-and I am putting the question to the Social Credit members-that Canada has known periods of intensive prosperity and of

The Address-Mr. Chevrier rapid expansion from 1896 to 1911, from 1921 to 1930 and from 1946 to 1956, under Liberal governments, without applying the Social Credit doctrine? How is it that these last few years, the countries of western Europe have been enjoying considerable prosperity and an accelerated development without resorting to Social Credit? How can the hon. member for Villeneuve explain these facts when in ours as in other countries, during periods of prosperity as well as of recession, the national income is always less than the national product?
Convinced that they have explained the cause of our economical problems by the difference between the national product and the national income, the Social Credit leaders claim that they can easily solve our difficulties. How? Simply by increasing the money supply and the credit so as to fill up the difference between the national product and the national income. Or again as the hon. member for Villeneuve states on page 61 of his book:
Social Credit consists in making the amount of money represent exactly the facts of production, and it is nothing else. No more and no less money than there are goods manufactured by Canadians. That is all we want.
And again, as he puts it in page 92:
For each dollar of products, there must be a dollar of purchasing power.
As I have just said, the cure put forward by the Social Credit members rests on a basic accounting error. But to this basic mistake, the hon. member adds another one just as glaring: he does not take into account the monetary turnover. It is an undeniable fact that money and credit are used several times, by changing hands, during a given year.
It is estimated that money has an average turnover of three times a year, which means that a given amount of money may serve during a year to buy three times as much products.
In 1961, for instance, the quantity of money in circulation remained at an average level of more than $14 billion, while our national production was valued at nearly $37 billion. How could we buy $37 billion worth of products with an average sum of money of about $14 billion? Simply by using that same money several times. So, the unbalance that Social Credit leaders believe to have found between the quantity of money in circulation and national production vanishes, once we take into account the monetary turnover.
Moreover, the inefficiency and failure of the Social Credit remedy has been clearly shown by the Conservative government these last

few years. From the beginning of 1957 to the end of 1961, the quantity of money increased by 32 per cent in Canada. During the same period, the national product, in constant dollars per capita, has gone down by 4 per cent. Therefore, this government had already done better than is asked for by Social Credit leaders, and yet, during that period of time, unemployment remained at 7 per cent.
All those facts show that the remedy suggested by Social Crediters is not any better than the explanation they give about our economic problems. They show also why Social Credit has never been applied in other countries. Major Douglas introduced the Social Credit theory about 40 years ago. The hon. member for Villeneuve would like us to believe that such a theory could save the world and easily solve all economic problems plaguing mankind; on the other hand, he is opposed to any planning system and to any nationalization project. But then, if the solution of our problems were as simple as Major Douglas seemed to indicate 40 years ago, how can one explain that he has not more followers in the world?
How can one explain that there is no government in the world nor a serious economist to accept the Social Credit philosophy?
How can one explain that most democratic governments, in France, in England and elsewhere in Europe, and more and more in the United States, are taking up planning, that Pope John XXIII is inviting statesmen to choose that direction and that no one in those quarters is interested in Social Credit? Are government leaders and all the most renowned economists of the whole world so ignorant or is it because they are in the service of commercial banks? Would Major Douglas and the hon. member for Villeneuve be the only ones to see the light and possess the truth? Or is it not simply that the hon. member is having visions, is being mistaken and is thus misleading the others?
In fact, the only concrete proposal which subsists in the Social Credit reform, is the fact that we should create as much money and credit as necessary to bridge the gap between national production and personal income, which would have corresponded, in 1961, to about $12 billion. Social Credit leaders would then have practically doubled the quantity of money and credit in circulation.
Such an experience would have been similar to the experience Germany went through following the first world war. We

all recall the disaster brought about by inflation in Germany. It ruined the middle class people and plunged the poor people in the depth of misery leading finally to the rise of Hitler, whom the hon. member for Ville-neuve seems to admire.
I should like now to say a word on the question of confidence in this government. During a television interview after the election, the hon. member for Villeneuve made the following promise to the whole Frenchspeaking population of Canada, and I quote:
If anyone comes up with a non-confidence motion, you may be sure that I will vote against the government whoever they are.
That was a definite and clear pledge. What has happened since? It is clear that the government has no intention of ending its austerity program and that it puts forward no efficient proposal to get the economy rolling again and check unemployment. On the other hand, the leader of the Liberal party has put forward a comprehensive program to improve the situation for all Canadians. He has further more moved a non-confidence motion against the government. The motion is simple and does not carry any principle unacceptable to the hon. member for Villeneuve.
Now, his colleagues rose one after the other, last night, to vote against the proposal, against the non-confidence motion, and no doubt I may assume that, if he had been in this house at that time, the hon. member for Villeneuve would have voted against the motion. The Crediter's vote clearly shows that either they are the allies of the Conservatives or they fear another appeal to the electorate; both explanations could be equally true. The implication then is that the hour of truth has come for the hon. member for Villeneuve and his colleagues. I am sure that those who voted for them because they were against a Conservative government have already passed judgment on them after their vote of yesterday.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to a series of fallacious, mendacious and untrue statements which I find in the book entitled "Real Caouette vous parle."
Here is what he says at page 17:
Tell me what the Liberals have given you over a period of 22 years, besides a war and a depression?
When the hon. member for Villeneuve asks such a question, he is falsifying the truth.
To begin with, it was not the Liberals who were responsible for the war, but Hitler, whom the hon. member for Villeneuve admires so much.
The Address-Mr. Chevrier
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that one of Hitler's slogans, from 1929 to 1932, was:
Sie haben nichts zu verlieren
"You have nothing to lose." They borrowed not only this individual's philosophy, but also his slogan.
Furthermore, it was not the Liberals who were responsible for the depression. The depression began in Europe and in the United States, and by the time it was felt in Canada, a Conservative government, under Mr. Bennett, was in power. It was not until 1935, under Mr. King's administration, that the Canadian economy picked up strength and, following the war, got started on the most rapid expansion period in its history.
Such is the kind of respect the hon. member shows for the truth when he speaks.
Again on page 27, he asks another question:
We have had the Liberals in Ottawa for 22 years; did they provide us with a steadily growing economy?
Further on, on page 35 he replies to that question:
You have tried the Liberals for years, and you have already tried the Conservatives for four years, but the results have been the same.
How can the hon. member for Villeneuve dare to deceive his fellow citizens in such a way? Either he is not aware that he is distorting the truth, and that is unforgivable for a party leader; if he is aware of it, then, he is not worthy of the trust he is seeking.
Let us consider the facts.
First, the economic field. We have experienced a constant economic growth over the 22 years of Liberal administration. Over that period, our country enjoyed the highest development rate in the world. Our national product, which was estimated at $5.6 billion in 1939, rose to $11.8 billion in 1945 and $30.5 billion in 1956. How can the hon. member for Villeneuve state that under the Liberals Canada experienced prosperity only during the war years?
But that is not all. The national product, in constant dollars and per capita, increased by 22 per cent between 1949 and 1956 but decreased by 4 per cent under the Conservative administration.
From 1949 to 1956, unemployment averaged 3 per cent of the labour force while under the Conservative administration, it averaged 6.5 per cent.
Since 1957, of all industrialized countries, Canada is the one whose economy experienced

The Address-Mr. Chevrier the slowest rate of growth. How can the hon. member for Villeneuve state that the Liberal and Conservative governments produced the same results?
But there is also the social legislation. Until 1957, the Liberals elaborated our whole system of social security: unemployment insurance, family allowances, old age pensions, pensions for the blind and the disabled, unemployment assistance, hospital insurance, housing aid, support prices for the farmers.
And you talk about respect for the dignity of man? Are there anywhere laws which have respected man and his dignity more than those?
It is true that in 1957 the Conservatives increased some pensions, but they did not introduce any new legislation in that field.
Here is another series of erroneous statements made by the 'hon. member for Villeneuve, at page 37 of his book. Listen to this:
Mr. Pearson was a member of a Liberal government in Ottawa from 1939 to 1945, a period of six years. During those six years, Mr. Pearson and the former federal ministers as well as the Liberal prime ministers of that time, went into debt, increased the national debt of Canada by $17 billion.
And a little further on, on page 38, the hon. member for Villeneuve continues:
-as for the national debt, an increase of $17 billion under the Liberals, an increase of $3 billion under the Conservatives.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how a member can so garble the facts and distort the truth as does the hon. member for Villeneuve in making such a statement?
First, I wish to remind him that, from 1939 to 1945, the leader of the present Liberal opposition was not a member of the government. He became a member of it in 1948 and from that date up to 1957, our national debt, far from increasing, decreased by almost $2.5 billion. Why did the member for Villeneuve fail to mention this essential fact? Indeed most other countries were getting deeper into debt during that same period while in this country our debt was decreasing. And why did he fail to compare that reduction of $2.5 billion with the $3 billion increase that occurred under the Conservative administration?
But even during the war, the net debt of our country increased from $3.2 billion in 1939 to $11.3 billion in 1945, which makes for an increase of $8 billion instead of $17 billion as stated by the hon. member for Villeneuve.


On page 20 of his book, the hon. member continues:
As a matter of fact, there are only two Canadian provinces where there is no provincial direct tax. And Alberta is one of them-
That is another lie, another falsehood. Indeed, I cannot believe that the hon. member is unaware of the fact that all provinces levy direct taxes and that Alberta, for one, collects income tax on corporations and private citizens, in addition to succession duties.
On page 91, I find this other quotation which the hon. member for Villeneuve repeated in his speech the other evening:
Mackenzie King said in 1935: As long as a country has no control over its money, it makes no difference who enacts the laws, because he controls nothing.
The hon. member went on as follows:
Unfortunately, Mackenzie King never did anything about it when he was in power in Ottawa.
That again is false. The hon. member for Villeneuve knows I hope, that the Bank of Canada controls credit and money in our country, and that it became the exclusive property of the state after 1935, thanks to Mr. King, and started to operate as such in 1937.
I could thus continue quoting indefinitely the numerous falsehoods which were repeated not only by the hon. member for Villeneuve but by several Social Credit leaders.

speechtext: All of them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Having forgotten the numerous benefits given to them by Liberal governments, after five years of Conservative mismanagement, the electorate believed the Social Credit's deceitful propaganda. They imagined that the Liberals had been just as bad as the Conservatives and they mistook the Socred leaders for men of good faith.
This kind of propaganda reminds me of the one used by the Conservatives, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, when they claimed before and during the electoral campaign, that everything was going well in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Besides the unjustified pretention that the Social Credit would have elected a great many members outside Quebec, and beside falsehoods he spread concerning the Liberal party in an effort to assimilate it with the Conservative party, the hon. member for Villeneuve also tried to convince

the people that the Social Credit doctrine was the only solution to their troubles. I trust I have refuted the arguments of that simple doctrine at the beginning of my remarks.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention another contradiction equally flagrant of which the hon. member for Villeneuve made himself guilty. At page 92 of his book, we find:
Under the present system-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is not his book.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Under the present system, the chartered banks create money and credit according to their whim and fancy. They create much of it in times of war and make it scarce in times of peace.
That quotation calls for several explanations. First of all, it is true that the commercial banks seek to make profits. But what is so disgraceful about that? It is precisely what private enterprise is looking for, this private enterprise which the member for Villeneuve and his Social Credit chiefs want to preserve and protect. Is the desire for gain a bad thing for commercial banks and a desirable one for other enterprises? Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely false that banks may "create money and credit according to their whim and fancy".
That statement might have been true when Major Douglas was writing, just after world war I, at a time when there was no central bank in Canada, but since 1937, in this country, it is the central bank that creates money and credit and determines the amount of currency, while commercial banks are reduced to the role of retailers.
Yet, in spite of this statement, Social Crediters continue and will continue to say that it is the commercial banks that "create money and credit in our country according to their whim" whereas the situation is completely altered since the Bank of Canada was established.
Besides, the member for Villeneuve contradicts himself on this vital question when he says, as can be seen on page 26 of his book:
Ladies and gentlemen, it is parliament which has entrusted to the Bank of Canada-and note this-the task of regulating credit and money. The bank is authorized by law to issue credit by the purchase of bonds from the government of Canada, the provincial governments . .. etc.
But then, if it is the Bank of Canada which is in charge of controlling credit and money, the chartered banks thus cannot create money and credit to their whim and fancy, as was claimed by the Social Credit leaders. We find there, right from the start in the Social Credit reform, a glaring inconsistency.
The Address-Mr. Chevrier
When the Social Credit leaders say that they would take away from the chartered banks the privilege of creating money and credit, on their own admission they intend to break through an open door because this has been the exclusive privilege of the Bank of Canada ever since 1937. All the chartered banks do at present, is to divide among their customers the credit created by the Bank of Canada, just as the automobile dealer allots to his customers, if any, the cars which have been sent to him by the manufacturer.
Like the hon. member, I should like-

The Address-Mr. Weichel

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a privilege to congratulate you and your deputy and chairman of committees, on your appointment to the important positions you hold in this house.
I should also like to express my sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Waterloo South, my next door neighbour and a very close friend of mine, and to the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska for their excellent speeches in moving and seconding the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Mr. Speaker, as the representative of a constituency which is a perfect blend of industry and agriculture, I am pleased and indeed elated at the proposals put forward to assist these two facets of our commercial and business life. As a member of parliament who has worked and fought for his country, I am also happy to hear of the plans to eradicate the major problems facing Canada. I am sure that our government has met these problems head-on with a view to improving the lot of each and every one of the 18 million Canadians and to making this country an even better place in which to live.
To my constituency the encouragement our expanding export program will receive means much. The bustling, thriving metropolitan area of Kitchener-Waterloo, as well as the surrounding smaller municipalities, cannot help but benefit from such things as the production incentives planned, the enlarging of the scope of the Export Credits Insurance Act and the industrial development bank. These agencies should be able to give valuable assistance to business, particularly in the essential task of expanding sales in foreign markets.
Plans for the establishment of a national economic development board I feel will be welcomed by my constituents, as well as by everyone in Canada who has the economic interests of our nation at heart. I am sure this board can serve a useful purpose in guiding private and public development.
While further budget measures are planned to meet our problems, the fiscal plans announced will, I am confident, create better employment opportunities for Canadian people, promote economic growth, strengthen Canada's balance of international payments and help maintain price stability. The farsightedness of our government is evident in the proposals to create new jobs over the coming years and to assist employers and workers in meeting the impact of automation. Such a broad attack on unemployment, one of our major problems for the past several

years as well as a giant-sized headache for our neighbours south of the border, will surely be hailed by industry and workers across the nation.
Our government, which has done more for the farmer than any previous government, has not forgotten him in this speech. The plan to convene a national conference on agricultural training this fall is a further step in improving the lot of the farm population.
While many people may have thought the issue of a national flag has been dropped, the speech shows that this is certainly not the case. As one who has spoken in this house on a distinctive flag, I am happy to see that moves are being made toward this end.
As everyone can see, the speech from the throne is extremely comprehensive and makes a determined effort to face the problems confronting Canada, whether they be economic or nationalistic. Our leader, Prime Minister Diefenbaker, could have played safe by keeping his legislative program as non-controversial as possible. Instead he has taken a bolder and more constructive course with a view to eliminating our difficulties. He has announced his intention of balancing the budget, a course which will improve our reputation among the nations and investors throughout the world. He has attacked the unemployment problem and aimed at strengthening the economy and boosting our export volume. He has outlined a variety of plans for improving the health of the country as well as that of the individual. He has also said he plans a budget which will attack even more of our problems.
Mr. Speaker, a little more than a year ago a bill was passed in the House of Commons and the other place to provide $5 million for physical fitness and amateur sport. This announcement caused a great deal of interest among the youth of our country and others. Our government was given high marks for bringing about this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, just before one o'clock I had mentioned that a little over a year ago a bill was passed by the House of Commons and the other place to provide $5 million for physical fitness and amateur sport. This announcement, as we all know, caused a great deal of excitement and interest among the youth of our country and others. Our government was given high marks for bringing about this legislation. Some time later 30 distinguished men and women

from across Canada were appointed to serve on the national advisory council on physical fitness and amateur sport to carry out the duties of such an important council. I mention this, as much good work has been done by this council up to the present time.
Perhaps one of the most important grants has been the one extended to the Royal Canadian Legion, dominion command, which provided funds for their program of expanding track and field activities through the facilities of a school for coaches representing every province in our country. I had the privilege of attending this school at Guelph, Ontario, which was under the supervision of Mr. Dyson of England, one of the greatest coaches in the world. In interviewing this fine gentleman I was deeply impressed with the set-up of such a program, and in talking to some of the athletes and coaches attending the school I found that in their view the benefits of training under this great coach were much greater than they had expected. They felt that with such coaching they could go back to their various training centres and teach these methods to the advantage of all sportsminded youth. I understand that the Royal Canadian Legion, the sponsors of the coaching school, are endeavouring to secure the services of Mr. Dyson on a permanent basis. If this effort is successful it will be a real step in the right direction.
From the grant that the Royal Canadian Legion received they provided some funds for the eastern track and field meet held last August in Waterloo, Ontario, and sponsored by the Legion branch of that city. This money helped to defray some of the expenses of bringing many athletes from every part of Canada. With nearly 500 of our youth participating in these events, this competition proved to be one of the best ever held in Canada, with many records equalled or broken. The Royal Canadian Legion branch at Waterloo in my riding deserves a great deal of credit for their wonderful efforts, and if some financial assistance can be forthcoming from year to year great strides will be made in track and field in Canada, with the important result that such efforts will help to build healthier bodies and healthier minds.
Before long Canada will again be sending a hockey team to compete with other countries for the world's hockey championship. I understand that with this in mind Father David Bauer of the University of British Columbia has brought forward a proposal to some of the members of the national advisory council and to the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association that such a team could be organized by the university where these players would have an opportunity of playing together for a longer period, something that has not
The Address-Mr. Weichel been done previously. Such a proposal should receive consideration by the council and the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association. The efforts of our government regarding this program, supervised by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith), along with the good work of the members of the national advisory council on fitness and amateur sport, are very commendable.
Some hon. members have mentioned the importance of education. May I say that most of my life I have been very interested in the three great assets of our youth, Christian training, education and recreation. For that reason I was pleased to receive the booklet "Youth Appreciation Week", an event to be held from November 12 to 18 and sponsored by the Optimist clubs. I believe the objectives in this booklet are worth repeating. They are:
To recognize the accomplishments of youth in the home, school, church and community.
To promote more active participation by families in family affairs.
To encourage groups and organizations to publicly show their respect for youth.
To encourage newspapers to devote more space to news of the 95 per cent of youth who are good citizens.
To encourage radio and television stations to recognize youth through special as well as regular programs.
To encourage national magazines to recognize the accomplishments and contributions of youth.
To provide the proper environment, recreation and social activities for youth.
To encourage parents to rededicate themselves to the responsibilities of parenthood.
To illustrate the great influence religion has on the lives of youth and to encourage their active participation in religious activities.
To encourage a greater interchange of ideas between adult and youth, leading to a broader understanding of the problems of each.
May we continue our advice and assistance to our fine youth in Canada, in the full realization that the youth of today will be the citizens of tomorrow.
In closing, I should like to say one word on another subject, Mr. Speaker. As one of the few retired civil servants sitting in the House of Commons, and one who gave nearly 36 years to the civil service commission under different governments, I am still very interested in the welfare of my former associates in this service. For many years the salaries of the members of this service could not be classified as extravagant. I can well remember when my salary was not as great as that of a foreman working in most industries. However, some improvements have been made by our government during the last four years, and I am pleased to see this. We pride ourselves upon having the best public service in the world. This is the result of the conscientious effort of most of these men and women in the performance of their daily duties. Thousands of such servants reside in my riding of

Perhaps one of the most important of these would be their loyalty to the civil service commission and the government. Disloyalty could well mean the loss of their position, as we all know.
The recent recommendations made for the federal public service outlined proposals for negotiation, conciliation and arbitration. I hope our government will give consideration to these recommendations at an early date.
I could mention the expansion and development of our industries and agriculture, as well as the universities in my riding. However, 1 know there are plenty of new members who would like to speak so I will cut my speech short. As noted previously, I am happy at the proposals in the speech from the throne. I am sure millions of my fellow Canadians feel similarly and will take part at the plans our government has outlined for the betterment of our great nation.

Mr. Speaker, my first words in this august assembly will be to congratulate you. Allow me to join with the distinguished and experienced members who preceded me in supporting also the unanimous decision of the house to appoint you to your present office.
I believe you are the first French-speaking Speaker to come from a province other than Quebec.
Since I come myself from New Brunswick, I especially rejoice in this great honour which reflects not only on you, Mr. Speaker, but also on all minorities in the other provinces of our country.
I should also like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Chaplin) and the seconder (Mr. Vincent) of the address. They performed very well their task which was difficult indeed. Needless to say that I do not necessarily share their views, but if I may recall a word by Voltaire:
I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.
My first duty, Mr. Speaker, is a very pleasant one; I wish to express my thanks to all my constituents. The people of Restigouche-Madawaska put their faith in me and I will always try to be equal to the task they have set me.
Mr. Speaker, while looking through the official reports for previous years and listening to the speeches of the members who spoke
[Mr. Weichel.l

before me during this debate, I realized that quite often, in their first speech, the members praise their riding's natural beauties.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that former members for Restigouche-Madawaska often had the opportunity of describing to you the enchanting decor of the Restigouche valley and of the magnificent republic of Madawaska which is situated along the fabulous Saint John river.
My immediate predecessors did not sit on this side of the house, but I am sure that, in the near future, I will be sitting on your right since that is the wish not only of my constituents but of all the Canadian people.
(Text):
However, Mr. Speaker, if I do not indulge today in a poetical description of the scenic beauties of my riding, I do wish to bring before this house the needs of my people. There is perhaps more unemployment in Restigouche-Madawaska than in any other part of this land. Last March the unemployment figures reached fantastic proportions and over 51 per cent of our major force was unemployed. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I still hear a voice saying-we cannot help but remember these words-"As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada no one, not one single fellow Canadian will suffer from unemployment." However, there are thousands of fellow Canadians in my riding who do suffer from unemployment and with this austerity program I am afraid that many, many more will be suffering great hardships. If the Canadian economy is booming, as we were told by many speakers from the opposite side, why not have some of it boom our way?
During the speech from the throne mention was made of the fact that the economy was booming indeed. I quote:
Economic activity in Canada has moved ahead sharply. This strong advance has resulted in more than 200,000 new jobs during the past 12 months. The objective of my government is to accelerate this pace of advance.
In order to accelerate this pace of advance in Restigouche-Madawaska, Mr. Speaker, there are a few local projects that should be proceeded with immediately, and I will deal with those projects very briefly:
1. A complete study of the fishing facilities in the Jacquet river area with a view to constructing additional wharves where needed. At the present time, local fishermen have to put up with a disgraceful situation.

2.	Crib walls at Charlo and Richardsville to keep what is left of the coast.
3.	A federal building with post office and R.C.M.P. tenements at Eel River.
4.	Wharf fill and storage shed for the Dal-housie federal wharf.
5.	Development of the Sugarloaf mountain in the Campbellton area or other suitable site for scenic and recreational facilities as a federal park.
6.	Immediate dredging of the Restigouche river off the Campbellton federal wharf as recommended by federal engineers.
7.	An airport in the lower end of Mada-waska county.
8.	Immediate start on the federal building in Edmundston for which land has already been purchased.
These are but a few of the federal projects which are vital to my riding and I strongly urge that they be proceeded with as soon as possible in order to provide work for the people now and possibly throughout the winter. Indeed I fear for the hardship and suffering which many of the people in Restigouche-Madawaska may have to endure this winter.
These are critical times and I expect the government to rise to the occasion and offer solutions for our national problems. But there was little in the speech from the throne to indicate that the administration intends to show initiative and positive leadership. That speech reminded me of an old ditty which is best applied in reverse-something old, nothing new; something borrowed, everything blue.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I was particularly surprised to read in the speech from the throne that we would be called upon to abolish the closure rule and to reinstate the special committee on procedure, because I believed that closure had been abolished some five years ago by the present administration. Was not the closure issue one of the main factors behind the victory of this administration following the pipeline debate? I was under the impression, Mr. Speaker, that the first move of the Prime Minister, after achieving victory, would have been to abolish closure. But to our great dismay, we find that nothing has been done in that connection, and that the rule of closure is still in force.
On the other hand, I was both happy and surprised to learn that the speech from the throne provided for:

The speech did not mention the causeway between Prince Edward Island and our province. This was, however, the last very solemn promise made by the Prime Minister on the eve of the prorogation of parliament. Will this development board, which is mentioned in the speech from the throne, be only another one of the numerous royal commissions set up by the government which travel throughout the country to look into problems and publish books which gather dust in the Prime Minister's office?
If it is this government's sincere intention to help the maritime provinces, there will be no need to set up a complex machinery which usually leads nowhere. If this government sincerely intends to help the maritime provinces, all that it needs to do is to start living up to the promises it has made to the people of those provinces over the past five years.
Let the government make an immediate start on the island causeway. Let the Chignecto project be put under way. Let it give more substantial aid to our provincial governments. Let it grant tax rebates to industries which locate there. Let local public works projects such as those I have just mentioned be put under way immediately.
Our people do not want more promises from the government; they do not want any more royal commissions to study problems. They are asking for some bread on the table and for the right and the opportunity for the head of the family to earn a living. What we want is to be on the same level, economically, as the other provinces in the nation. We simply want a place in the sun, as first class citizens. (Text):
The great majority of the Canadian people, 63 per cent of them, showed on June 18 that

The Address-Mr. Dube they had no confidence in the present administration. In New Brunswick we doubled the number of our Liberal seats, and now that we know the truth we shall do even better in the next election, which I hope will come soon.
During the election campaign the government succeeded in hiding the financial crisis Canada was in, and government spokesmen were telling the people, as I said before, that the economy was booming. On June 14 the Prime Minister stated this on television:
We have bared the record. We have concealed nothing. We have shaded nothing.
Those of us who held the opposite view were called prophets of doom and gloom. Yet, on June 24, six short days after the election, the Prime Minister was forced to go back before that same television screen and finally tell the people the truth, disclosing the financial crisis which he had been hiding and announcing his austerity program thereby creating, for the first time in modern Canadian history, as I believe was said yesterday, extra taxation and legislation by television. On that ground alone, on the ground of having concealed the truth, the Prime Minister has lost the confidence of the nation.
Duly elected members of this house, whatever their political affiliations may be, have a moral duty not to support what is contrary to our Canadian principles. Last night we all saw what took place, a strange and fantastic alliance coming together, the Social Credit members to my left and the social debit members to my front. If those two go on sleeping together too often they will lose what is left of their respective reputations.
Another breach of our most sacred parliamentary rights was the refusal to call parliament into session as soon as feasible after the election. This should have been done, first to seek a vote of confidence from the house and, second, to advise the house as to what position this government intended to take at the commonwealth conference.
I submit that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) took the narrow view at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference. He failed to adapt his mind to a changing world. He took the old line Conservative approach when the world was crying for broad, modern Liberal thinking.
The free nations of Europe for the first time in modern history are trying to unite themselves for their common good. They are succeeding. The common market is the first step in the ultimate goal which is one free Europe united in peace and prosperity. Who are we, or who does the Prime Minister think [Mr. Dube.l

he is, to sail across the seas and to wave the red flag of the past in an effort to stop the traffic of the future?
This is the second half of the twentieth century, yet our present Canadian government would have us chained and shackled to trade patterns which were obsolete even before they were born.
To be sure, we want to keep the commonwealth alive; but we want a progressive and prosperous Great Britain, and Great Britain cannot, in my humble opinion, become progressive and prosperous outside the common market. It is obvious to any mind-that is, to any mind which can accept and digest reform-that once the common market walls go up around free Europe, the "tight little island" will be left behind and miss her opportunity to soar into the future with her prosperous neighbours. It is our duty to help Great Britain join the new club. We don t want to be tied to her apron strings, yet we don't want to be her ball and chain. Great Britain's entry into the twentieth century club will ensure her prosperity and at the same time will provide us with a prosperous market for our exports.
Above all, Great Britain's entry would satisfy us that the British experience in democracy can become a cornerstone in the new building. The free nations of Europe could use some of the stability and political maturity of English statesmen who were born in the shade of Westminster and brought up by the mother of parliaments.
To help Great Britain into the common market should be our first aim. Our second purpose should be to secure for us, for Canada, closer economic ties with the European economic community.
We already have NATO, thanks to the broad approach of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, a real man of vision. Why does not the present administration wake up and sponsor a new form of North Atlantic Treaty Organization to deal with the present challenge? Why not organize all the nations of the Atlantic area, not into a market but into a super market? Perhaps the present antiquated Conservative administration is not aware that over the past few years the supermarket has replaced the corner grocery store. The corner grocery store is still handy after hours, and perhaps on Sundays, but the price is better and the price is more varied at the supermarkets. In the days of the Right Hon. Mackenzie King and in the days of the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, when our present leader, (Mr. Pearson) was secretary of state for external affairs, Canada had a strong and persuasive voice in the councils of the world. Canada was not only the link between Great Britain and the United States; she was also

the leader of all the small powers of the world. Our then secretary of state for external affairs was accepted as one of the world leaders whose advice and good common sense was sought by all. If I may say so, Mr. Speaker, as I look across to the opposite side of this house I see no further material for the Nobel peace prize.
In the speech from the throne I saw nothing which could add even an idea to the international field. From the point of view of foreign affairs, as well as from the point of view of national affairs, it was an empty speech.
The world around us is changing and changing fast. The United States of America have elected a new, young, dynamic president. The modern nations of Europe have united to form a common market and are forging ahead, but our present leaders are standing still! They have nothing to offer; their sole ambition is to hang on to their seats.
The plane is flying in all directions and they fasten their safety belts while asking the taxpayers to tighten their austerity belts. So we are all belting in a state of fantastic confusion.

Besides, I am convinced that if each one of us visited his constituency, he would get the same answer: what we want is work; what we want is a solution to the unemployment problem; what we want is work for our people so that they may earn their living honourably in Canada, a country which is overloaded with wealth and which is able to provide a living for everyone.
Mr. Speaker, for those reasons, and since it is the people's wish, we, the Social Credit members, are asking without any political partisanship that the government introduce in Canada a vast public works program, a program which, from coast to coast, will serve to attune this country to the rhythm that twentieth century progress can allow.
There are hospitals, colleges, universities, bridges, roads and several other things that should be built. And yet, even if we have the necessary materials to build all those things, even if we have the steel, the labour and the engineers, even if we have the asphalt, the bricks, the plaster etc. for all that, our government seems to prefer to leave our people unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, we suggest there is a way of carrying out those projects while leaving at the same time the provinces free to act in their own areas. But the government should then see to it that the Bank of Canada becomes, not only the bank of the central government, but also the bank of the provinces and of the municipalities, in other words, the bank of the whole people, so that the provinces may secure from the Bank of Canada interest-free loans to carry out those projects


which are essential to our country; this not only will enrich our people, but will also contribute the development of their security and their freedom.
Mr. Speaker, there are many projects which should be carried out at the federal, provincial, municipal and school board levels. But strange as it seems, the governments nearer to the people, those with the most urgent works to carry out, are precisely those with the least income, while the central government, which is farther away from the people, grabs the largest share of the taxes. The municipal government, the most important one as far as the private individual is concerned, the one closest to him, the one which has to build streets, waterworks, maintain fire and police departments, carry out maintenance work, is the one with the fewest sources of income.
The federal government's responsibilities towards the private citizen are much smaller, less important. And, what matters even more, the government which is closest to the private citizen, while it has many projects to carry out, does not have the money to perform the work. Why not let him go to the Bank of Canada, or to the municipal development bank, to try and secure an interest-free loan so that it may build the things it needs.
When you see a municipal council holding a meeting and ratepayers asking the mayor, the aldermen, for a road, a street to be paved, a sewer to be built, a water system to be installed, not a single alderman raises his hand to ask where the asphalt, the machinery, the engineers are to come from. None of them puts that question. All raise their hands to ask where to get money to build this road or these waterworks.
The same thing happens at the provincial level. There are delegations coming to meet the minister of health to request the building of a hospital which is needed so that sick people can be cared for locally. What is the government's answer? We have no money. Always the same answer. If, instead of being asked to build a hospital, these people were asked to build a bank to pile up dollars in it; would it be different? That is the whole thing: no funds.
Mr. Speaker, upon careful reflection, we wonder why, if we have men smart enough to ensure the progress that we witness today and to invent the machines used to develop our country as it is nowadays, why those

very men are completely unable to attune our monetary system to the present realities, to changing conditions.
That is important today, Mr. Speaker. We know that our engineers have discovered amazing production techniques. Our people have courage and are willing to work, but something is lacking: this token, this little note which will allow them to achieve economically what is physically possible.

The Address-Mr. MacEachen responsible for my return to the House of Commons than the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) who, as leader of the Liberal party, has striven mightily and successfully to put the Liberal party in a position to provide an alternative to the present truncated ministry.
The Leader of the Opposition has served his country in war and peace with nobility of spirit and great distinction and it is surprising to me that this morning the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) should have developed the line he did. Is the Leader of the Opposition or any other member of the House of Commons to keep silent when the mistakes and follies of this government lower Canada's reputation and tarnish her good name?
Is the Leader of the Opposition to remain silent when the relations of Canada with other friendly countries are worsened because of the conduct of ministers? Are these men who identify themselves, even as a minority government, with Canada to be immune from criticism? How vain and thinskinned can you get? This morning the Secretary of State for External Affairs complained of smearing; and this from a gentleman who, in a speech in Vancouver, suggested, or hinted or implied, that Premier Khrushchev was working for the Liberals in the last election, from one who, with his colleagues, dared to attack our party and its leader by saying that we wished to ruin our country if we could not rule it. A man who has said that should step silently and softly when he talks about defamation.
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring the house back for a moment to the night of June 18. On that night the people of Canada rendered their verdict on the conduct of the present government. The issues had been presented to the people of Canada in a long and vigorous election campaign. The results are evident: the government was defeated at the polls, it lost the confidence of the majority of Canadians, and it suffered the greatest haemorrhage of government supporters in the history of Canada. Even though the government was demoralized, even though it had lost the confidence of the people of Canada, the government had to carry on. The Queen's government must go on. The very first thing, so we are told, that the government had to face was a crisis in foreign exchange of major proportions. We believe, Mr. Speaker, that the actions of the government on previous occasions and its wrong policies were responsible for that exchange crisis. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) told us last night that it was a minority government that caused the run on the dollar. Well, that is a new theory which will be added to the theory

on international exchanges; a theory on the same level of sophistication as the view that sun spots cause depressions.
The government was faced with this exchange crisis and it took action. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in a statement to the people of Canada stated that action was necessary to save the dollar. Action was taken and embodied in an order in council which the Prime Minister said was within limits approved by parliament; that he was acting with authority given to him by parliament. The order in council that put into effect sweeping emergency measures rests on two statutes: the Customs Tariff and the Financial Administration Act. One part of the order in council removes the application of the British preferential and intermediate tariffs and accordingly raises the level of tariffs to the general tariff. The second part of the order in council utilizes the Financial Administration Act to relieve individuals in the country from the operation of the first part of the order in council.
Does anybody, Mr. Speaker, in his right mind believe that the statutes on which this order in council is founded were intended to allow a government to take extraordinary and sweeping action to avert a further depletion of Canada's reserves? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) very properly questioned yesterday the legality of this order in council. I am not a lawyer and I certainly do not intend to argue the legality or the illegality of the order in council. But I will say that the government was certainly straining very hard when it chose these two statutes upon which to base this particular sweeping measure. We have had very impressive legal advice suggesting that this order in council is indeed illegal, and that all the regulations and activities carried on under the order in council are consequently illegal. We have had that opinion. The Minister of Justice said that it is completely legal. I do not want to argue that point, but I do want to say this, Mr. Speaker, that once the government had taken this emergency action embodied in an order in council, its first constitutional obligation was to bring parliament together, to bring the elected representatives of the people together, so that they could exercise their traditional and cherished rights of dealing with the taxation that is imposed upon them. Mr. Speaker, the government were obliged to call parliament together. We say that they should have called parliament at the earliest possible moment, even without a crisis, even without emergency and sweeping measures being taken. We say that surely, in the midst of a national emergency, the first obligation of a ministry that had lost the confidence

of the Canadian people, that did not command a majority of the House of Commons, was to call parliament together and give the elected representatives of the people a chance to exercise their constitutional rights.
Mr. Speaker, in this country for over 100 years we have enjoyed the benefits of responsible government. We know that responsible government is not prescribed by any specific statute; rather it is a principle of the constitution that sustains and supports the statutes. In Great Britain, for example, since 1688 the responsibility of the ministers to parliament has been enforced by certain various specific legal requirements. The legal requirement or the constitutional requirement that concerns us now is the requirement that the ministers shall neither collect nor expend moneys without the expressed authorization of parliament. This requirement is of absolutely first rate importance to our democratic system, and that requirement was not fulfilled or lived up to by the present government. During the 17th century when the system under which we live was worked out in England there were doubts about parliament's absolute right in the field of taxation but all these were settled conclusively by a provision of the bill of rights of 1689 which declares as follows:
Levying money for or to the use of the crown by pretence of prerogative without consent of parliament for longer time or in other manner than the same is or shall be granted is illegal.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this order in council which is now the basis for these sweeping measures has been put into effect by the government presuming to itself the pretence of a prerogative. We know that later on in the United Kingdom great deference to this principle is illustrated by a decision of the House of Lords in the case of the Attorney General v. Wilts United Dairies. In this case it was decided that the crown could not collect taxes under a statute which did not clearly and expressly confer on the crown that right. I ask hon. gentlemen if they will point to a single part of the statutes under which they are operating which clearly and expressly confers on the crown the authority which they presume in the order in council.
Professor Hood Phillips of Gray's Inn, in his standard work on "The Constitutional Law of Great Britain and the Commonwealth" has written as follows:
It has been settled law since the early seventeenth century that the King in Council has no power to make laws for the realm except as a delegate of parliament. Perhaps the most significant application of this principle lies in the rule that no person or body other than parliament... can raise taxes or spend public money, for it was round that issue of taxation that the earlier struggles between King and Parliament mostly raged.
The Address-Mr. MacEachen
Sir Erskine May, an authority frequently quoted in this house, makes the same point:
The crown demands money, the Commons grant it, and the Lords assent to the grant: but the Commons do not vote money unless it be required by the crown; nor do they impose or augment taxes, unless such taxation be necessary for the public service, as declared by the crown through its constitutional advisers.
Another authority, namely Eric Taylor in his work "The House of Commons at Work", states as follows:
Underlying all the financial procedure of the house are certain ancient maxims or rules, some of them the prize of centuries of struggle with the crown.
He then goes on to enumerate these maxims, and the first of them is as follows:
(1) the granting of public money, and the imposing of taxation, is the function of parliament, not of the the Queen or the government.
This order in council which has not come before parliament-and we have no indication that it will come before parliament- collects and imposes taxation. May I end this reference to authorities by referring to a quotation from Edmund Burke on this point, referring to this struggle to establish this very principle, namely the right of parliament to impose taxation:
They took infinite pains to inculcate as a fundamental principle, that in all monarchies, the people must in effect themselves, mediately or immediately, possess the power of granting their own money, or no shadow of liberty could subsist.
I suggest that the action taken by the cabinet through the sweeping measures in imposing taxation violates this fundamental constitutional principle as parliament has not been given any indication that it will have an opportunity to approve this action taken by the government.
If I may, I should like to refer to a Canadian illustration in order to indicate how jealous the House of Commons is of its right to collect money and impose taxation. In 1914, to deal with the emergencies of a great war, parliament enacted the War Measures Act. That act is still on the statute books of this country as our chief statutory provision for wars and insurrections. It permits the governor in council to do almost everything that the governor in council may deem necessary. Yet in 1939 an interdepartmental committee established to examine the effects of this War Measures Act found that under this act no government could impose taxation without the authorization of parliament.
This principle is very important because even under the War Measures Act the government cannot arrogate to itself the authority which it arrogated to itself under the order in council to which I have already referred. Yet the great defence of the procedure followed in this instance was to go
