The Address-Mr. MacEachen back to 1947 and to say that the Liberal government of that day was obliged to impose sweeping measures as it did, that it imposed these measures under an order in council and that "We are doing the same thing; what is wrong with it?"
I wish to tell hon. members what my investigation has revealed concerning the procedure followed in 1947. It is true that Mr. Abbott on the radio made an announcement about these extraordinary measures. But in his speech, a copy of which I have before me, he has this to say:
Now that the government's proposals have been announced, we propose to follow the usual budgetary practice of asking parliament-
I emphasize the words "of asking parliament".
-to make them effective from the time of announcement, and taxes at the new rates will therefore be collected on all sales by manufacturers and on imports, beginning tomorrow morning.
In that announcement Mr. Abbott advised the Canadian people that he would be laying these measures before parliament at the earliest possible opportunity. Parliament met at the earliest possible opportunity, namely on December 5, 1947, and what do we find from the speech from the throne? We find these words:
Provision of a temporary character has been made to conserve and supplement Canada's reserves of United States dollars.
The measures recently announced to deal with the various aspects of the immediate foreign exchange difficulty will be submitted for your approval.
To parliament. That was in the speech from the throne. When parliament met the then prime minister, Mr. King, asked permission to interrupt the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne to bring in these measures. The leaders of the other parties wanted to exercise their right to make speeches on the address in reply. This was on a Friday, I think, and Mr. King told the house that on the following Thursday Mr. Abbott would introduce those measures in the House of Commons so that parliament would have an opportunity to deal with the measures which Mr. Abbott had announced on the radio on November 17.
How different in this case. The Prime Minister in his statement on television on June 24 made no reference to submitting these measures to parliament, not a word, not a gesture.

He told us to cool off. Now we get the speech from the throne, and you can search it word by word and you will find not a single reference to an opportunity being provided to validate the action taken by the ministry. Is there any mention of


legislation? Have we seen anything on the order paper? Nothing. That is the difference between the present action and the Liberal action in 1947. At that time the action was announced and parliament was brought together. We had a majority government then. We did not have a government depending upon the unstable whims of a minority group in the House of Commons; but that majority government brought the legislation to the House of Commons for approval.
What did hon. gentlemen of the Conservative party, some of whom are in the ministry today, say on that occasion even though Mr. Abbott had brought legislation into the house to validate , his actions? Here is what one hon. gentleman, the present Prime Minister demanded to know of one minister on December 11, 1947. He said to the minister as found at page 189 of Hansard:
Can he tell me in any country of an occasion where taxation has been imposed by a minister, by order in council?
That was the Prime Minister who asked that question in 1947 when he had an opportunity to debate and approve the action taken by the government. Later, as found on page 408 of Hansard of December 17, the present Prime Minister had this to say:
Did something happen on November 17 that made it necessary for this government to depart from the time-honoured procedure of having parliament called together for the purpose of having budget proposals presented in a legal and constitutional form?
If the right hon. gentleman could make the welkin ring in 1947 when parliament was given an opportunity to debate a number of proposals, it is no wonder that hon. members of this house should feel outraged at the action of the government in not even intimating that we are going to have an opportunity to deal with these sweeping measures.

After what happened in 1947 the Liberals should choke on the citations just quoted. It is particularly gratifying to me to represent the constituency of Royal because of the fact that for 25 years the government leader in the Senate served his people and New Brunswick as a fine representative of this constituency. The fact that I succeed him has made it doubly pleasant for me because of the residue of good will which still surrounds his name and his record of public service in this place. I also wish, Mr. Speaker, to pay tribute to your thoughtful yet fair guardianship of the rules of this house, without which it seems to me it could rapidly rival the tower of Babel of ancient times. The mover and seconder are now basking in an aura of well merited tribute for the manner in which they began this historic debate. May I, too, pay tribute to them.
Now, I have one other compliment I wish to pay, and it is to the former minister of justice. As a lawyer and a former provincial legislator I have had many opportunities of knowing his unique contribution to the better administration of justice in Canada. The national parole board, the new enlightened penal policy, including the establishment of minimum security facilities, are but one or two aspects of the forward looking reforms for which this country is the better. The justice ministry is not a popular portfolio in the fickle imagination of the public. Nevertheless, the Hon. Davie Fulton is entitled to recognition for the special qualities he brought to this department.
If I could classify and isolate a single impression, Mr. Speaker, after a week as a member of this house, it would have to be that words, and their ordinary plain meaning,
The Address-Mr. Fairweather are really not very ordinary, neither are they plain. They seem to take on shades and partisan connotations. Now, perhaps this is all very well in this house, although somehow I doubt it. But it does seem to me it makes our supposed dialogue with the public a bit complex. In addition, I am one of those who believe that words should be jealously treated.
May I illustrate this by reminding the house that during our Prime Minister's visit to London last month the Leader of the Opposition in a particularly unpatriotic and uncharacteristic way, said that Canada's attitude was little more than carping criticism. Then, in his speech on Tuesday last the Leader of the Opposition, among many other criticisms of Canada's stand in London, said that this government exhibited its peculiar genius for getting into unnecessary difficulty with its friends. In the Guardian of Manchester on September 12, the well known correspondent Patrick Keatley wrote this:
The prime ministers and the presidents hurled verbal thunderbolts but they did it with courtesy, precision and a marked lack of excess emotion or phony histrionics.
In a lead editorial entitled "The Reality of Consultation" a few days later the same newspaper said:
Mr. Macmillan has made a powerful case for British entry into the common market. Equally the commonwealth prime ministers have made a strong case for questioning the terms so far provisionally agreed in Brussels .. .
The editorial ends in this way:
It is a little frightening that, in all the volume of British press comment and public discussion, there has been so little talk of the commonwealth's detailed anxieties. Rightly the government (of the U.K.) and much of the press have emphasized the gains to be won by British entry into Europe. Rightly, too, the risks of staying out have been recalled. But we must also listen to what the commonwealth says-and not just brush it aside as due to domestic politics or unreal fears. Not long ago Conservatives in this country (U.K.) complained because others were supposed to have advocated "unconditional" entry into Europe. Today, ironically, it is the government (of the U.K.) that would like a blind eye turned to these conditions.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit this evidence of the effectiveness of our Prime Minister's contribution at London last month. The point of the conference, after all, was not just to join hands and sing patriotic airs but to see if Messrs. Heath and Macmillan could be forced to demand better terms at Brussels. After all, was this conference meant to be a sterile thing? Was there to be no frankness, no exchange of genuine points of view? For what it is worth, I happen to share the view expressed by the Canadian trade committee in its study of this subject entitled, "The Impact

The Address-Mr. Fairweather of European Integration on Canada." This is a most useful short statement prepared by Mr. Dana Wilgress.
It seems to me that Canada has, in fact, adopted the United States approach in facing the challenge on a regional basis. This will result in some form of trading area with the United States. The great legislative victory won by President Kennedy in the senate recently is good news for Canada and is recognized as such in this government. I think Canada is ready to accept the challenge and, as Mr. Wilgress wrote:
This will involve many difficulties in making the adjustments that become necessary. The stimulus afforded by this necessity may make Canada a stronger nation and a nation better fitted to achieve its destiny.
But it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, we must keep in mind that the common market means more than a united Europe the common market means a common tariff. Before that wall is built around Britain, surely Canada is entitled to some collective bargaining.
The throne speech contains three items that I have selected as being of special interest to the people of the Atlantic part of Canada. First, there is the fact that the program of rehabilitation and development of agricultural lands is proceeding actively and that we will be asked to provide funds for it. I am a great believer in the potential of ARDA. I think it is a great program, a great concept and, to use a word that has been abused in this house, I think it is concrete evidence of a great vision. My only concern is that up to now its potential has not been effectively put across to our farm people. The program should be talked about across this land with the zeal of an evangelist because its potential result could literally save rural Canada.
The national economic development board brings to Canada a pattern that is well established in western Europe, but may I suggest that it cannot work here without the voluntary support of labour and management. It also depends on their enthusiastic participation in the planning process. This is the crux of the program and one which must be free of petty political manoeuvering and petulant staged exits of those who must share in the common responsibility for economic and social development.
I shall next deal with another board which has been sought in the Atlantic provinces for many years and is now a part of the evolving pattern of this government's support for the three maritime provinces and Newfoundland. It is the Atlantic development board which has been unanimously welcomed by the press in Atlantic Canada. I am sure that if it is rapidly established and gets down to its job it

can make a great contribution to the solution of our economic problems. This approach towards regional decisions for regional problems has long been part of the British government's policy, and also has been in vogue in France. It has helped to solve economic problems in Wales and Scotland, and I believe it can be of great help to eastern Canada.
However, I would hope that, in addition to the setting up of this board, greater flexibility would be provided in our banking system which would allow cash and credit to be made more readily available in different parts of Canada. I have not given full study to this matter and do not know which particular statute would require amendment, but the federal reserve system in the United States carries out this principle to good effect. In the United States they have an adaptable and flexible policy which has proven to be of beneficial effect. Canada is so large that different antidotes are sometimes needed to take care of various regional problems, and I am sure hon. members would agree that there is no inflation in Atlantic Canada, and very little danger of it.
The establishment by the United Nations and the Food and Agricultural Organization of a world food program must touch the imagination of Canadians, and the fact that this program is the result of Canadian inspiration and initiative must be a cause of modest satisfaction to hon. members. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) so eloquently reminded us the other evening, two thirds of our people in the world are hungry. The fact that Canada proposes to share in a positive program based on a recognition of this human fact should be proof of our intention to do our part in the solution of this world problem. We have actively responded to a need which is ageless. Missions are already crossing the world to catalogue priorities, and we will soon be asked to make proper appropriation in supplying Canada's contribution.
Step by step we have evolved in this land from dependence to independence, and now the road is open to interdependence. I can think of no finer memorial to the late Dag Hammarskjold than the fulfilment of one of the causes he so effectively championed.
Might not the next step be a program outlined in the September 1 edition of the Illustrated London News by Sir Arthur Bryant? In it Sir Arthur writes:
In certain strictly defined and limited cases, where new production of real wealth urgently needed by mankind can be accurately gauged and measured, I feei that it would be possible, without causing any inflationary tendency, to attach to the production of certain forms of universally required wealth, notably the production of mankind's chief need, food, the equivalent creation by the state of interest-free capital which would enable the

undernourished peoples of the world to absorb the surplus and exportable food production of countries whose peoples are already consuming all the food they require.
Perhaps such a bold program might be part of Canada's adaptation to the changed conditions resulting from Britain's participation in the common market.
My final observation has to do with the national power grid, one more of the visions about which my hon. friends opposite delight in ridiculing the Prime Minister. New Brunswick already knows how beneficial it is to be on a grid with Nova Scotia, and how useful it is to be able to sell surplus power to the adjacent state of Maine. I could never quite understand all the hubbub about the Columbia river, because we have found it most useful and beneficial in New Brunswick to be able to export power to the United States.
To me one of the bright prospects for the Atlantic region, and in particular for the coal mining industry of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, is a national power grid. In one instance it might utilize power from the Columbia and in another power produced by the Hamilton falls in Labrador. It would also be greatly effective in utilizing thermal power generated from the burning of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia coal. This vision is no more unrealistic than was Macdonald's for a cross country railway, and this vision could mate-realize into exporting much more electricity into the power-hungry United States. After all, power lines know no artificial boundaries.
As this debate has progressed it seems to me that speakers have vied with each other in declaring how important is this session of parliament. Let us prove it to the country by proving it to each other.

Regardless of whom it was written by, it was an excellent speech. It was well delivered, and I say in all sincerity that Canada and the Liberal party are indeed fortunate that a young Canadian of such unusual ability has seen fit to continue a long line of public service that was begun by his distinguished grandfather, Sir Michael Cashin,
The Address

Mr. Nicholson more than 50 years before Newfoundland entered confederation. As a young man I knew Sir Michael Cashin and I am sure he would have been singularly proud with the efforts of his grandson in his first appearance in this chamber.
A new parliament has just opened-a parliament which is faced with grave and challenging problems. The way in which we address ourselves to these questions will affect not only the welfare of Canada but the welfare of peoples in many other nations. I firmly believe that the standard which the people of Canada will apply to this parliament will be an exacting one, and we should govern ourselves accordingly.
Mr. Speaker, as was drawn to the attention of this house when you recognized me, I, like Saul of Tarsus, come from no mean city. I come from Vancouver, a city which I am told by all who know it is not only one of the most beautiful but also one of the most progressive in Canada. It is also one of the most cosmopolitan cities in Canada. Many of its residents are immigrants and the children of immigrants. We have in Vancouver several thousand Chinese Canadians many of whom have won distinguished places in the life of our community, on the staffs of our universities and in other fields. We have several thousand Canadians of Italian, Greek, Scandinavian, German and Japanese origin. But the great majority of the inhabitants of this city are of Anglo-Saxon, Scottish or Irish descent. Vancouver is also the financial and commercial centre of British Columbia and is one of Canada's greatest seaports. The riding which I have the honour to represent, Vancouver Centre, is in the heart of metropolitan Vancouver. It is the core of a population of approximately 800,000 people. Vancouver, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, is on the west coast of Canada far removed from this capital. What I would like you to understand however, is that I come here as a coast-to-coast Canadian. I wish to assure this house through you, Mr. Speaker, that it will be my endeavour not to indicate any degree of sectionalism or any undue partisanship in points of view to which I may give expression from time to time. Undoubtedly I shall be partisan at times. After all I ran as a Liberal and I am proud of my party and of our leader. I trust, however, that I shall not be unduly partisan.
Having made my position clear, I now wish to say that, in my humble opinion, the first duty to which this parliament should address itself is the recovery of its prerogatives and powers. In June, 1956, I returned to Canada after an absence of some five years in South America. I had occasion to be in Ottawa in the early summer of that year and I followed

The Address-Mr. Nicholson with unusually close attention the proceedings in this house at that time. I did so partly because of my close association with the petroleum industry of Canada through the Polymer Corporation during its first 10 years, and also because of an extended stay in South America where political traditions and practices differ greatly from ours. In several of the Latin-American countries that I have visited, the army plays a most important part in government. It has been said, with some degree of truth, that the army is the greatest democratic force in several of the Latin-American republics. Apart from the army, however, there have been presidents and other national leaders whose viewpoints are extremely nationalistic and who have been highhanded and dictatorial in the way they run the affairs of their countries.
With such a background, it was not surprising that I should follow with unusual interest the matters which were being discussed in this house in the early summer of 1956. In the course of my visit and during the several months that followed I heard several hon. gentlemen, who now occupy front bench seats on the government side, speak in an impassioned and dramatic way about the rights and responsibilities of this house.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) proclaimed time and again in 1956 and 1957, both in and out of the house, that the rights of the members of this house were being ignored and trifled with. I say in all seriousness that the arbitrary, dictatorial actions of the present government during the months which have elapsed since the election in June last are far more deserving of censure and condemnation than anything which took place in the spring and early summer of 1956, especially in the light of subsequent events. Again you will note, Mr. Speaker, it was this same Prime Minister who, in 1958, 1959 and 1960, boasted that he had restored the honour and the prestige of parliament.
Our leader, in his magnificent address on Monday last, dealt effectively with the government's failure to give our nation the leadership needed at this time. He dealt with their failure to implement many of the promises and assurances given in the course of the campaigns in 1957, 1958 and again in 1962. He also referred to the exposure of matters which should have been brought to the attention of the electorate before the election took place but which the people were kept from knowing through the deliberate action of the government in order to win votes.
I had not intended to even refer to what our leader said on these subjects. I would not have done so had it not been for certain things mentioned by the Secretary of State


for External Affairs (Mr. Green) this morning and also by the Prime Minister in the course of his remarks on Tuesday. He said in effect that never in the history of the country had there been such unjustified and unwarranted remarks made in the course of an election campaign and in this house about a government and its leader.
My comment on this statement is that never in the history of this country have the actions of a leader or of a government called for such condemnation. They should be condemned if for no other reason than many of the statements made in the course of the recent election campaign and for making a mockery of their boast that they had restored the rights and prerogatives of this house. As an example of wild and extravagant statements made in order to win votes, I intend to read a few quotations for the benefit of the house. This is what I was criticized for this morning. It was said that I had made wild and extravagant statements in order to win votes. But can hon. members think of anything more extravagant than the statement made by the very minister who made this accusation in this house earlier today? In Hamilton on May 17 the Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
When James Coyne left his post as governor of the Bank of Canada, tight money went too.
How absurd.

Prime Minister in Edmonton on May 26, as reported in the Edmonton papers. I am now quoting from a newspaper.
At Ottawa on May 29 the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) said this:
We are enjoying in Canada today one of the greatest periods of expansion in all Canadian history. We've achieved in Canada a remarkable stability in the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar.
And the dollar had gone, in a period of months, from a premium of $1.05 to $0.92 and a fraction.
Mr. Speaker, this morning I was criticized in this house for having told the truth that Canada's prestige and reputation had deteriorated greatly since the present government took office. I still believe that to be the case. It has deteriorated, as evidenced by the following articles. In Maclean's magazine, the issue of January 6 of this year, there is an article by Hannon referring to, and quoting from, British periodicals and newspapers of that time. It is headed: "Why even the tolerant British don't like us anymore". I am not going to read the whole article, but the third paragraph begins:
By year end, responsible London newspapers like the Times and the Observer were carrying reports accusing Canada of deliberately trying to obstruct the British entry into the Common Market and of rudeness and discourtesy at the diplomatic level.
Then again further down in the same article:
British annoyance really boiled over though when Finance Minister Donald Fleming insisted on the full text... of a speech by the Lord Privy Seal, Edward Heath... No doubt unintentionally Fleming gave Britons the impression that he thought the full text would be significantly different from the summary he had already received- that is, that Britain was trying to deceive her commonwealth partners and sell them out in secret. When the text was finally published, and turned out to be no more than a clear statement of the well-known British position, Britons stopped trying to conceal their indignation. "Inexcusable", said the Manchester Guardian, and the Daily Herald added:	"Heath is now due for some Canadian
apologies".
1 happened to be in Britain last year, Mr. Speaker, when this agitation was going on, and I was confronted every day with articles in the newspapers and also with comments from people I met from time to time.
The situation still continues. I refer now to an article in the Washington Post on September 17 of this year. The Washington Post says:
-Commonwealth countries, including Canada, probably won't succeed in keeping Britain out of the common market, though it may succeed "in boring the rest of the world with the pettiness of some of their complaints".
The New York Times, one of the finest newspapers in the world, says:
The Address-Mr. Nicholson
-the Commonwealth countries are staging a "virtual revolt" against the mother country at the prime ministers' conference in London.
In an editorial it says the conference issue "lies between Prime Minister Macmillan's dynamic world-wide 'grand design', which takes account of modern economic trends, and the separate and even parochial trade interests of the Commonwealth countries".
The grand design ... calls for Britain's entry into the European economic community "on the basis of the same imperative consideration that created the community".
"As Mr. Macmillan explained, a modern economy can no longer prosper within the narrow confines of a small national state when economic power is shifting to units of continental proportions".
In contrast, the editorial says, the commonwealth countries fear both a potential dissolution of the commonwealth and, more immediately, serious injury to their economies due to an extension of common market tariffs to Britain and loss of the imperial preference for their goods-
The British government is still determined to press ahead ... but the vehemence of the commonwealth opposition is bound to strengthen British domestic opposition.
And lastly the Daily Mail, during the conference in early September of this year, accused the Prime Minister of sulking because of hurt pride in politics.
Mr. Speaker, if anyone should tell me, when you find articles of that nature published in leading newspapers in the United States and leading magazines and periodicals in Britain, that the prestige and international reputation of Canada has not suffered, I would be a very surprised man. Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I was accused of making an unthruthful statement and was criticized for it, but I said nothing more than the truth. To me, Mr. Speaker, a new member in this house, it is a shocking and deplorable thing that a government, having made extravagant and irresponsible statements such as those mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition when he reviewed the life of this government, and such as those I have read, which in spite of these misleading statements was beaten at the polls, should insist upon carrying on. To me it is an even more shocking thing for the government to adopt the attitude that it did at the recent prime ministers' conference. The Prime Minister, who had been beaten at the polls, saw fit to go to London purporting to speak for Canada without calling this house together to ascertain how the members felt. Is that the conduct that you would expect from a government which says that it has restored the rights and prestige of parliament?

Responsible government is the foundation of our democratic institutions. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I would be gravely remiss in my duties as a member of this house if in my first utterance in debate I did not

The Address-Mr. Nicholson express my opinion of the government's complete disregard of this basic constitutional principle of responsible government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like in the balance of the time at my disposal to deal with the speech from the throne. It is noticeable not so much for what it says but for what it fails to say. There is a sad lack of any clearly-defined program for this session, and a complete failure to recognize that if the economy is to boom again measures must be taken to stimulate growth and production in the nation's industries. Attention has been drawn to the fact that no mention whatever is made in the speech from the throne of Canada's important fishing industry. But what is even more remarkable is that no mention whatever is made of Canada's most important industry, the forestry industry. There is no mention of forests, forestry or forest products in the whole of the speech from the throne. There is a passage to the effect that the government will reintroduce some legislation eliminating or correcting discrimination in the logging tax, but apart from that there is no mention whatever of any intention to improve matters or conditions in the nation's most important industry. And yet, Mr. Speaker, one out of every 12 Canadians working in the nation's goods manufacturing industries is concerned with forestry and the manufacture of products from our trees.
Of all the manufacturing industries in this country the forest industry stands first in employment, first in terms of wages paid, in new investment and in net value of output. Approximately one third of Canada's total export earnings come from the sale of forest products outside of our boundaries or approximately $2 billion a year. Yet in the speech from the throne there is to be found not a word of what the government intends to do to help this industry. It is not only important to the province of British Columbia, where 50 cents of every dollar comes out of the forest industry, but it is also important to the economies of New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Quebec and other provinces.
This industry has serious problems. During the question period yesterday I referred to one of them, namely the move on the part of the lumber industry in the United States, which is by far our most important market, to reduce through a quota arrangement lumber imports from Canada. A hearing opened before the United States tariff commission in Washington earlier this week on a petition lodged by the lumber manufacturers of the Pacific northwest. Vancouver, Ottawa, Toronto and other Canadian papers have made extensive references to this inquiry. The Vancouver papers are full of it. These articles all


highlight one thing, namely that the prime thing that is actuating these Americans in their request is the fact that the Canadian dollar has not only been devaluated but has been pegged at 92J cents. The United States manufacturers put this fact forward as their basic case. They contend that this devaluation of the dollar constitutes a built-in tariff wall. While admittedly the forest and other Canadian industries have gained some temporary advantages from the "pegged" devaluation, the tables are now turning. As the leader of the Liberal party and other spokesmen on this side of the house have been saying for weeks, the tables are now turning and this move of pegging the dollar which has resulted in the built-in tariff is now becoming a matter of grave concern to Canadian lumbermen and other exporters.
I had hoped, Mr. Speaker, that my old friend the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) would be in the house today, as I should like to have congratulated him upon his appointment as Minister of National Revenue. As an old friend I congratulate him on the appointment and I wish him well in the tough spot in which he finds himself because of the government's austerity program. However, in congratulating this new minister upon his appointment I know I voice the feelings of the forest industry in all parts of Canada that it is a matter of grave concern that this government is so short of good men that one man is obliged to handle two of the most important portfolios.

It seems to me that when parliament in its wisdom decides that there should be a department to look after the welfare of the nation's most important industry, the importance of that industry warrants the appointment of a full-time minister to look after it. When the Department of Forestry Act was passed great stress was laid on research. In fact, three of the five subsections which define the powers of the minister deal with research. In the light of the stress that was placed on research, it is a matter of great regret that, as to the research program which the industry hoped for, no action is being taken upon it. Research is urgently and vitally needed in the forest industry in this country. One has only to go back, as some of my friends in the far corner will recall, to the time when hemlock was a waste product in British Columbia, good for little more than a firewood. Suddenly as a result of research it has become a valuable product in the manufacture of high quality pulp and paper. Cedar is equally a wood that was discarded. Eighty per cent of all the

red cedar in the North American continent is in the forests of British Columbia. Only 75 per cent of the cedar is being cut because there is no economic use for the older trees. The matter calls for extensive research. Yet little has been done in that regard.
While -in the speech from the throne reference is made to the fact that the government is going to give the big corporations some tax incentives in order that they may carry on further research, what are they doing for the small businessmen? What are they doing for the loggers in British Columbia, with their stands of cedar, who have these problems to solve? Nothing is being done in that regard as they cannot get any benefit out of these tax incentives. Speaking here on behalf of the small operators in all parts of Canada I say that it is high time the government did something about research in this important field of forestry.
I might say that I have a soft spot in my heart for research because during the 15 years that I was in industry, nine and a half of them in the Polymer Corporation, we plowed millions of dollars into research. Think of the handsome dividends that are being paid today on the money that was timely spent at a difficult time in the history of the Polymer Corporation.
If we were to arrange the large nations of the world today in order of their strength, virility and effectiveness, in either peace or war, we would find a similar order if we were to substitute for effectiveness the total national expenditure a nation makes on scientific research.

Mr. Speaker, one of the trials under which I suffer now in returning to parliament after four years absence is the long unwieldy title that has been attached to my constituency. I cannot help thinking that it is a typical Conservative action, namely as much as possible to smother reality in words.
In coming back to this chamber after four years absence I must confess that I have been assailed with the disconcerting thought that in spite of the rapid pace of events in the world outside, here is some strange cloud-cuckoo land in which time stands still. What do I find, Mr. Speaker? I find our old friends the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition still brandishing their wooden swords, waving their cardboard shields, fighting the mimic battle all over again as they did previously, as they were doing when I left here in 1958. I suppose one can say there is something quaint, amusing and entertaining in
The Address

Mr. C. Cameron this stylized performance; but to me there is something dismaying and disturbing in the flippant and frivolous manner in which these two eminent gentlemen discussed the problems of the nation, if that is what they were doing, on the highly intellectual plane of "You're another", obviously more concerned not with how Canada's affairs are to be conducted but with who is to get the job of conducting them.
My hon. friend, the leader of this group and member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge), remarked the other day on the strange fact that the Liberal and Conservative parties can examine the same set of statistics and come up with diametrically opposed conclusions. I am equally impressed by the manner in which these two great parties regard certain dates in history such as the year 1957.
The Liberal party, of course, regards the year 1957 as a date hardly less significant than the fall of man when our first parents were expelled from paradise. Ever since, of course, they have been standing wistfully at the gates, like houris at the gates of paradise, hoping again to be admitted to the green gardens. On the other hand, the Conservatives, of course, regard 1957 in much the way in which the leaders of the revolutionary movement, the liberation movement, regard the anniversary of the day on which they led the forces of liberation to victory, and like such liberators they have a tendency, of course, to imagine that by harping on the horrors of the previous government people will tend to overlook the horrors of the new one.
Being neither a Liberal nor a Conservative I have a different view of 1957 and I rather suspect it is the view that history will take of that doom-laden year. I rather suspect that history will regard 1957 as the year in which the Canadian people awoke from a long uneasy slumber, shot by the occasional nightmares of 22 years of Liberal rule, and that when they awoke, rubbed their eyes and regarded the spectacle of the results of those 22 years they went stark, raving mad and elected a Conservative government.
I am interested in the way in which both the Liberals and Conservatives would have one believe that the year 1957 was a sharp cut-off date at which everything changed. Of course, if one examines the statistical record one finds that there is not even the slightest irregularity in the dismal curve down which we have been descending for the last decade. This government's incompetence, and heaven knows that has been well proven in the last five years, is not so much in having created a crisis as in having been unable to cope with the crisis already created by their Liberal predecessors.

The Address-Mr. C. Cameron
In fact, I wonder sometimes, Mr. Speaker, if the well known occult powers of the late prime minister Mackenzie King may not have descended to his successors because they would seem to know when it is advisable to lose an election, and I wonder whether the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Piekersgill) may perhaps be the custodian of that crystal ball. I must say that it was one of the brighter moments of my life the other day to hear the honourable and irrepressible member for Bonavista-Twillingate, standing arrayed in the white robes of purity, washed in the waters of repentance, with not even a smidgen of oil from the trans-Canada pipe line soiling the hem of his garment, reading us a lecture on the evils of cynicism in public life.

speechtext:
However, sir, I must not fall into the error of the two great political parties and rake over old and rather malodorous straw. We have to regard what is now proposed for the future by these two great parties of Canada and, of course, if we refer to the throne speech we have some difficulty in discerning just what that program may be. I note that it is one of the aims of the government to adopt measures to develop the Canadian economy, to maintain a high level of employment, to strengthen the balance of payments-all very laudable aspirations. Unfortunately, the rest of the speech does not


reveal that the government has the slightest idea of how to achieve these laudable purposes.
One of the points in the throne speech that particularly interested me was the matter of incentives to our shy and diffident business community. I would have thought that the present all too generous depletion and depreciation provisions with regard to oil, petroleum and minerals would have been enough to encourage even the shyest entrepreneur to proceed on his way in making profits. But no, we give him some further incentives. I was particularly interested to notice that some help is to be afforded to the hard-pressed forest products industry of British Columbia, about which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Nicholson) was speaking a few moments ago, because I recall that just a few days before I left the Pacific coast to come to Ottawa two of the largest lumber corporations in Canada were indiscreet enough to report that in the first half of 1962 their profits had increased over the same period in 1961 by 43 per cent and 50 per cent respectively. If this is part of the belt tightening process, then all I can say is that it is going to be a highly selective process. But I am quite sure that those of my constituents, of whom there are a great many who work in the forest products industry, who are members of the international woodworkers of America and the pulp and sulphite workers, will be greatly interested in this gesture toward their employers, particularly as they have recently signed a no-pay-increase agreement on the basis of the stringencies affecting their industry.
We all know, of course, that our Prime Minister is a very devout and pious man but it does seem to me that it is carrying piety to extreme lengths to undertake to implement a policy on one scriptural adjuration alone, namely, "to him that hath shall be given and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath". I have observed that spokesmen both for the Conservative party and for the Liberal party are apparently hoping to overcome our present discontents by re-establishing patterns of the past that have been irretrievably shattered. It is a truism, of course, that we live in an age of revolutionary change, but unfortunately a great many of our people, perhaps a majority, are unable to accept the fact that this truism is in actual fact the plain unvarnished truth. The confusion perhaps arises from a misuse of words or a misunderstanding of words, perhaps a semantic confusion. To all too many people the words "revolution" and "revolutionary" conjure up visions of Fidel Castro or communist conspiracy or people with bombs and beards plotting in basements

when in actual fact the revolutionaries of the twentieth century are to be found in other places. They are to be found in our laboratories, in our technical and engineering institutions. They are being urged on in their revolutionary work, of course, by the self-styled opponents of revolution.
They, of course, themselves would be horrified to hear themselves described as revolutionaries. However, they are the real revolutionaries of today and all our problems of today result from the revolutionary activities of these people about whom we hear very little. The European common market, balance of payments, the grim and rising tide of unemployment, the shattered trade patterns, all these arise from the work of these revolutionary forces in our midst. I would suggest, sir, it is time we in this house recognized this revolution and realize that sooner or later throughout the world we have to establish revolutionary institutions to match this technological revolution which is taking place.
I am among those who find it literally impossible to believe that 18 million people in possession of the largest per capita natural wealth in the world are able to produce poverty without the exercise of the utmost ingenuity. We have not lacked ingenuity to date. We have, indeed, been more than ingenious in devising stumbling blocks in our way. In the meantime, we have to face some immediate problems. I suggest to you, sir, we are not going to face them by attempting to re-establish institutions, patterns and customs that have now been shattered beyond repair.
Let us take this question of export trade of which we hear so much from all sides of this house. While the objective of the division of labour throughout the world and the specialization of production between the different economies of the world is undoubtedly a desirable and commendable objective, surely the spectacle of 18 million people allowing themselves to drift into the position where they depend for the elements of their daily living on their ability to force on other people their surplus goods, while at the same time rejecting and resisting as far as possible the efforts of others to force their goods upon us, speaks of inspired lunacy. There is mounting evidence, I suggest, that we are not going to be allowed to pursue these lunatic paths much longer, even if we choose to do so. It is painfully evident that something else must be done. Let us, by all means, export what we can of our surplus products. Let us, by all means, find all the customers we can. But let us recognize that the day is gone when we are going to live in Canada in the lap of luxury, trading in traditional patterns.
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron
We are approaching the end of the age of pack rats, as someone has described this age in which the energies of the human race are devoted to transporting materials back and forth across the face of the globe. May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in facing these problems we might well take a look at our own Canadian history to see if a study of that history may not give us a solution for our immediate problem. I am always surprised and somewhat dismayed to hear the statement made, as it is made plainly and bluntly in the throne speech, that Canada's development will continue to require imports of capital, a statement in which I believe the Liberal opposition concur. This is an approach that I completely reject on two grounds. The first is that it is demonstrably false, and the second that it is an encouragement of the continuation of a process that has almost brought us to the brink of disaster.
I think that this is the time when we should begin to grow up. I have noted in recent months in the newspapers rather acid and pointed comments by various authorities in different parts of the world about Canada's infantile and regressive determination to remain in a state of economic infancy. Some very sharp things have been said about Canada and Canadians persisting in regarding themselves as an undeveloped economy in desperate need of help from abroad. I suggest to you, sir, that our history gives the lie to that position.
I should like to take you back, sir, some 20 odd years, to a time when we faced even more dangerous and difficult days than we face at the present time. In 1939 we were faced with the problem of playing our part in a war to exterminate the nazi disease that was creeping over the face of the globe. It is rather interesting to see what we did on that occasion. In fact, I think we sometimes forget the almost miraculous force of that war effort, the astonishing achievements of those years from 1939 to 1945. At that time, from the depths of the depression, with an industry grinding to a halt, almost overnight we transformed ourselves.
Now, there will be those who will say, it is all very well to go back to the days of war, but we cannot do that again. For one thing, people will say, look at the enormous volume of debt that was created. I want, first of all, to deal with this question of the necessity for importing capital which every member, even those who advocate the import of capital, fully recognize is fraught with great danger.
In 1939, the rate of capital formation in Canada stood at $754 million. Only three years later, in 1942, it had risen to a rate of

The Address-Mr. C. Cameron $1,556 million. We will be told, of course, that the people of Canada endured all manner of hardships and restrictions during the war, and cannot possibly be asked to undergo them again. Well, statistics do not bear that out because I find that personal expenditure on consumer goods and services rose from $6,510 million in 1939 to $9,261 million in 1945. Then, we are told, of course, as I say that we would only add to our mounting debt. I have some figures that cast not only a revealing light on what occurred at that time but also what has occurred since those days of the war.
In the depths of the depression in 1933 and 1934 the charges on Canada's national debt consumed over 8 per cent of our gross national product. Throughout the whole of the war, when an enormous war production program was being carried on, when standards of living were being raised throughout the country, the carrying charges on Canada's national debt remained almost constant at just over 4 per cent of the gross national product. Here, perhaps, is an indicator, Mr. Speaker, of the truth of what I said a few moments ago, that the crisis in which we are involved today had its genesis long before the advent of this unfortunate and incompetent Conservative government. I find that back in 1955 the carrying charges on Canada's debt had dropped to 1.8 per cent of the gross national product. In 1957 they went even lower to 1.6 per cent of the gross national product, and last year they had only risen to 2.1 per cent of it. Therefore I suggest that there is ample leeway for a vast expansion program in Canada without any dangers whatsoever of the sort of inflationary pressures which many fear, or any dangers of an overwhelming burden of public debt.
For that reason I would recommend to the government and the Liberal party that they should divert some of their attention from trying to re-establish broken patterns of conduct and behaviour and seek an outlet elsewhere.
If it was possible for Canadians to place their economy, as we did, at the service of the war to defeat nazism, is there any reason today why we cannot place the Canadian economy at the service of providing for the raising of living standards throughout the world? Is there any reason whatsoever why the Canadian government cannot plan, and inaugurate a planned program of production to meet the needs in capital goods of the underdeveloped areas of the world, and do it by long term low interest or no interest credits? Even if we were never repaid we would be in no more difficult or dangerous position than we were during the war when all this vast expansion of production was consumed


by the Canadian people in the sense that it was paid for by them, and in the process Canada refound prosperity. I would suggest that this is the great task of the present age.
We have become so involved, mentally and psychologically, in the absurdities and horrors of the cold war, in mutual bomb rattling and bomb testing, and in mutual suspicions, that we are overlooking the fact that this cold war, with the possibility of its erupting into a hot war, is already becoming a thing of the past; that there is another war that is beating on our doors today, and that is the war against hunger, misery and ignorance throughout the world. That is a much more dangerous war. It is a war which, if we lose it, will have as disastrous consequences as any that might come from a nuclear explosion.
Here we have the vast majority of the human species, because remember we members of an affluent society are only a small proportion of the human species, living in conditions which we would consider intolerable deprivation and hardship, and one of the reasons for the revolutionary actions I was speaking about is that today, for the first time in history, two things have happened. One is that we have conquered the problem of production. We know now we can create material abundance, and the other is that, also for the first time in history, human beings in every part of the world are made aware, by sight and by sound, of the way in which other human beings live in other parts of the world.
It is one thing to hear vague rumours that people on the other side of the world live in comfort and luxury while you yourself live in poverty, but it is an entirely different thing to see a picture of these affluent people on the television or movie screen. The vast bulk of the have-nots in this world are not long going to be content. They want to come into the twentieth century.
Here, I submit, is a golden opportunity for a country such as Canada to place our economy-our developing economy, and let us not be silly and place ourselves on the same economic level as Ghana-in the forefront of a drive to combat this misery. We are a developed economy. We can generate our own capital, we have done it before. So let us advance now on this much more important war, this war for human freedom, this war for human decency, this war against misery.
Would not this lay the foundation for a real clarion cry of advance, a call to arms to which every Canadian could respond with good heart? It would give our nation that thing which everyone says we need desperately, a sense of national purpose, and it would give each individual Canadian one thing that every individual requires, a sense of spiritual purpose.

This, I submit, is the challenge of the twentieth century, and this parliament and this nation will fail that challenge at their peril.
